title: Next Number With a Divisible Digit Product
statement:
You get two positive integers n and t. Return the smallest integer that is at least n whose decimal digits multiply to a number divisible by t.

n itself counts if it already works. A product of 0 is divisible by every t.

examples.why: 23 gives 6, not divisible by 4. 24 gives 8, which is.
31 to 36 give 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, none divisible by 7. 37 gives 21.

hints: How far can you possibly have to search before a product becomes 0?
Within any 10 consecutive numbers, one ends in 0, and its digit product is 0. So a plain upward scan stops within 10 steps.
Write a helper that returns the digit product, then try n, n + 1, n + 2, … and return the first one whose product is divisible by t.

explain.intuition:
This looks like it needs number theory, but a short observation makes brute force safe. Every run of 10 consecutive integers contains one that ends in 0, and any number with a 0 digit has product 0, which every t divides. So you never check more than 10 numbers.

Once you know the loop is short, the clean answer is the simple one: check n, then n + 1, and so on.
steps: Write digitProduct(x): multiply the digits by peeling them with % 10.
Return x. The loop runs at most 10 times.
pitfalls: Starting the search at n + 1. The answer may be n itself.
Treating a 0 digit as "skip it" instead of making the product 0. Then 10 would get product 1 instead of 0.
Overthinking it: trying to build the answer digit by digit when the bound of 10 steps already makes scanning optimal.

complexity.time: O(log n), at most 10 numbers of O(log n) digits each

solutions.title: Scan upward
solutions.idea: Check n, n + 1, … with a digit-product helper. A number ending in 0 appears within 10 steps, so the loop is short.

followups: t can be as large as 10^14 and n is a string of 200 000 digits. Why does scanning break, and what changes when t has a prime factor above 7?
Return the count of numbers in [n, m] whose digit product is divisible by t.
